title: Bladder Stones
subject: Surgery
summary: Bladder stones are hard urinary deposits that form in the bladder, common in low‑resource settings due to infection, dehydration and outlet obstruction. Diagnosis relies on bedside clues and bedside ultrasound, and treatment focuses on stone removal and addressing the underlying cause.

sections.p: A bladder stone is a solid mass of mineral salts that has formed within the bladder lumen. Diagnosis is clinical plus imaging, usually bedside ultrasound; plain X‑ray is used if ultrasound is unavailable.
b: Hard, mobile mass felt on suprapubic palpation
History of recurrent UTIs, hematuria, or obstructive voiding

t.b: Confirms presence, size and number of stones; also shows residual urine and hydronephrosis. If unavailable, use a plain KUB X‑ray.
Detects infection and crystal type; guides antimicrobial choice.

sections.p: Severity is graded by stone size, number, and presence of complications such as obstruction or infection.
b: Small (<1 cm) – may pass spontaneously
Medium (1–2 cm) – usually requires endoscopic removal
Large (>2 cm) or multiple – may need open cystolithotomy

sections.p: In low‑resource settings the most frequent causes are infection‑related and obstructive.
b: Schistosoma haematobium infection – common in bilharzial regions
Chronic bacterial cystitis – especially with Proteus or E. coli
Bladder outlet obstruction – BPH, urethral stricture, prostate cancer
Dietary factors – low fluid intake, high oxalate or purine diet in children
Foreign bodies or indwelling catheters

sections.p: Patients present with lower urinary tract symptoms and sometimes visible blood.
b: Suprapubic pain or discomfort
Intermittent gross hematuria
Dysuria, frequency, urgency
Incomplete bladder emptying, post‑void dribble
Recurrent UTIs

sections.p: Investigations aim to confirm the stone, assess size, and identify the underlying cause.

t.b: Shows echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing; also evaluates residual volume.
Detects radiopaque stones when ultrasound not available; may miss uric acid stones.
Identifies infection and crystal type; guides antibiotics.
Assesses kidney impact and guides peri‑operative care.

t.a: Schistosoma serology or urine ova exam (if endemic)
t.b: Detects schistosomal infection; positive result prompts praziquantel therapy.

sections.p: Complications can become life‑threatening if not addressed promptly.
b: Acute urinary retention – requires immediate catheterisation
Severe infection/sepsis – fever, tachycardia, hypotension
Bladder wall erosion → fistula or squamous cell carcinoma (schistosomiasis)
Hydronephrosis → renal impairment

sections.p: Treat the stone, eradicate infection, and correct the underlying cause.
b: Acute retention: Foley catheter, monitor output
Antibiotics: cover common uropathogens; avoid nitrofurantoin if renal impairment
Stone removal: cystoscopic lithotripsy or percutaneous suprapubic cystolithotomy for large stones
Address obstruction: BPH medical therapy (alpha‑blocker) or surgical relief if needed

sections.p: Prevent recurrence by correcting modifiable risk factors and monitoring.
b: Repeat ultrasound at 3 months to ensure clearance
Hydration counseling – aim for >2 L urine output daily
Treat any persistent infection; consider periodic urine culture
In endemic areas, annual praziquantel prophylaxis
Manage BPH or stricture definitively

sections.p: Conditions that mimic bladder stones on presentation or imaging.
b: Bladder tumour – may also cause hematuria; ultrasound shows solid mass without acoustic shadow
Urethral calculus – located proximal to bladder neck, not within bladder
Clotted blood – can appear echogenic but lacks shadowing

sections.p: Certain tests may give false‑negative or ambiguous findings.
b: Uric acid stones are radiolucent on KUB; may be missed without ultrasound
Early schistosomal infection may have negative ova exam; serology helps

faq.q: Why are bladder stones more common in children in developing countries?
faq.a: Children often have low fluid intake, high‑oxalate diets and may suffer from recurrent infections that promote stone formation.

faq.q: Can a bladder stone cause cancer?
faq.a: Chronic schistosomal infection with bladder stones increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

faq.q: What if ultrasound is not available?
faq.a: A plain KUB X‑ray can detect radiopaque stones; clinical suspicion and urine analysis guide management.

exam: What immediate step do you take in a patient with acute urinary retention due to a bladder stone? — Insert a Foley catheter, assess post‑void residual, and start antibiotics if infection suspected.

How would you differentiate a bladder stone from a bladder tumour on bedside ultrasound? — Stones produce a bright echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadow; tumours are solid masses without shadow.

A 7‑year‑old boy from a rural area presents with hematuria and a palpable suprapubic mass. What is the most likely diagnosis and why? — Bladder stone; common in dehydrated children with poor diet and recurrent infection.

Which infection is uniquely linked to bladder stones and bladder cancer in East Africa? — Schistosoma haematobium; its eggs irritate the bladder wall, promoting stone formation and squamous carcinoma.
If a stone is larger than 2 cm but the centre lacks endoscopic facilities, what is the recommended management? — Open suprapubic cystolithotomy under regional or general anaesthesia.
Why should nitrofurantoin be avoided in a patient with bladder stones and impaired renal function? — It requires good renal clearance; accumulation can cause neurotoxicity.
What laboratory finding would prompt you to start praziquantel in a patient with bladder stones? — Positive urine ova for Schistosoma haematobium or positive serology in an endemic area.
How does chronic bladder outlet obstruction contribute to stone formation? — Stasis of urine promotes bacterial growth and crystallisation, leading to calculi.
